title: Egypt Struck and Healed: My People, Egypt
summary: The LORD rides on a swift cloud into Egypt, and its idols tremble. Egypt falls into civil war, its Nile dries up, its industries fail, and its famous wise men give foolish counsel, until it is handed over to a harsh master. Then the oracle turns: in that day Egypt will speak the language of Canaan, build an altar to the LORD, cry out and be rescued, be struck and healed, and join Assyria and Israel in worship as a blessing in the midst of the earth.
story: Chapter 18 ended with distant Cush bringing gifts to Zion. Chapter 19 turns to Egypt, which the Cushite kings now ruled, and which Judah's leaders kept trusting as a shield against Assyria. The first half of the chapter dismantles that trust: Egypt's gods, river, economy, and wisdom will all fail. The second half is among the most astonishing passages in the Old Testament. Egypt, the house of slavery from which God rescued Israel in the exodus, experiences its own exodus story, crying out under oppressors and receiving a savior. And Assyria, the empire threatening Judah at that very moment, is named alongside it as God's own. The next chapter returns to the present, with Isaiah walking barefoot as a sign against Egypt and Cush.
historical:
In the eighth century BC Egypt was divided. Several rival dynasties ruled different parts of the land, especially in the Nile delta, a period historians call the Third Intermediate Period. Verse 2, with city against city and kingdom against kingdom, fits this fragmentation well. The Kushite king Piye marched north and subdued the rival rulers around 728 BC, and his successors ruled all Egypt as the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty. Zoan (Tanis) was a royal city in the northeastern delta, and Memphis (verse 13) was the ancient capital near the apex of the delta. The harsh masters and fierce king of verse 4 have been identified with the Kushite conquerors, with the Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, who invaded Egypt in the 670s and 660s BC and sacked Thebes around 663 BC, or with later conquerors such as the Persians. The text names no one.

The second half of the chapter looks to “that day” and is harder to tie to one period. Jewish communities did settle in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 43 and 44), and a Jewish military colony at Elephantine on the southern border had its own temple in the fifth century BC. In the second century BC a Jewish priest named Onias built a temple at Leontopolis in the delta, and the historian Josephus reports that he justified it by appeal to this chapter's altar in Egypt. Many scholars date some of verses 16 to 25 later than Isaiah for these reasons, while others hold that the prophet foresaw the nations' conversion in a vision that no later event exhausts.
cultural:
Egypt's life depended entirely on the Nile. Its annual flood watered and fertilized the fields; a low flood meant famine. Verses 5 to 10 trace the effect of the river failing: canals stink, reeds and papyrus wither, fishermen with hooks and nets have nothing to catch, and the linen industry collapses. Egypt was famous for fine linen woven from flax grown along the river, and textiles were a leading export. The whole economy, from the rich to the hired laborer, would suffer.

Egypt was also famous for its wisdom. Its scribes produced instruction literature, collections of counsel for officials, some of which resemble parts of Proverbs. Isaiah mocks Pharaoh's counselors for their claim of ancient and royal lineage. The spirits of the dead, mediums, and spiritists in verse 3 reflect the Egyptian concern with the dead and with consulting the unseen world. A pillar (verse 19) was a standing stone set up as a memorial or boundary marker, and an altar in the middle of the land with a pillar at its border would mark Egypt as territory belonging to the LORD, as Israel's own patriarchs had set up altars and pillars in Canaan.
literary: The chapter falls into two halves. Verses 1 to 15 are poetry announcing judgment, moving from Egypt's gods and politics (verses 1 to 4) to its river and economy (5 to 10) to its wise men (11 to 15). Verses 16 to 25 are prose, built on five sayings each introduced by “In that day” (verses 16, 18, 19, 23, and 24), and they escalate from terror (verse 16) to worship (verse 21) to an equal share in blessing (verse 25). The second half deliberately echoes the exodus: Egypt cries out because of oppressors, the LORD sends a savior, he makes himself known, he strikes with a plague and then heals. What God once did to Egypt for Israel's sake he will do in Egypt for Egypt's sake. The final verse gives Egypt and Assyria titles previously reserved for Israel.

outline.t: The LORD comes to Egypt: idols tremble, civil war, a harsh master
The Nile fails and Egypt's economy collapses
The folly of Pharaoh's wise counselors
In that day Egypt fears the LORD's plan
Egypt learns the LORD: an altar, a savior, a plague and healing
A highway from Egypt to Assyria and a threefold blessing

doctrines.note: The chapter pictures Israel's two great enemies worshiping Israel's God and sharing Israel's titles. God's purpose for the nations is not only judgment but inclusion, with Israel as a blessing in the midst of the earth, as promised to Abraham (Genesis 12:3).
God strikes Egypt with a plague, but the purpose of the blow is healing. Judgment here serves repentance: they turn to the LORD, and he hears and heals.
Egypt's renowned wisdom fails because it does not know what the LORD of Hosts has planned. True wisdom begins with God's counsel, not with human cleverness or ancient pedigree.

Egypt's idols tremble when the LORD comes, and in its confusion it turns to idols and spirits of the dead. The chapter exposes the powerlessness of the gods of the ancient world's most religious civilization.

words.note: Etsah, counsel, plan, or advice. It appears four times in the chapter. Egypt's counsel is frustrated and its wise men give senseless advice, while the plan of the LORD of Hosts stands (compare 14:26). The contrast between human and divine counsel runs through Isaiah.

Rapha, to heal. Verse 22 uses it twice: he will strike them but heal them. The same God who healed Israel (Exodus 15:26) promises healing to Egypt. The pairing of striking and healing presents judgment as a means to restoration.

Matstsevah, a standing stone or pillar. Jacob set one up at Bethel (Genesis 28:18), but the law later forbade pillars used in pagan worship (Deuteronomy 16:22). Here the pillar marks Egypt's border as belonging to the LORD, a witness rather than an idol.

Nachalah, inheritance, the portion that belongs to someone. Israel is the LORD's inheritance throughout the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:9). In verse 25 that title remains Israel's, but Egypt is called My people and Assyria My handiwork, names that had marked Israel's special relationship with God.

christ: The New Testament does not quote this chapter directly, so its link to Christ is through the pattern it sets out. God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him, and Isaiah pictures that promise reaching Israel's oldest oppressor and its present enemy. The early church saw that hope begin to take shape when Gentiles from every nation were brought into the people of God through Jesus the Messiah (Ephesians 2:11-19). The savior sent to Egypt in verse 20 is not identified in the text, and reading it as a direct prophecy of Jesus goes beyond what it says, but the chapter's movement from striking to healing and from enemy to people of God is the shape of the gospel. Matthew even applies Hosea's words about God calling his son out of Egypt to the child Jesus (Matthew 2:15), showing that Egypt itself had a place in the story of the Messiah.

hard.q: Has verses 18 to 25 ever come true, or does it describe the future?
hard.a: Readers give several answers. Some point to history in stages: Jewish communities in Egypt from the sixth century BC on, the Greek translation of the Scriptures (the Septuagint) produced in Alexandria, and later the rise of Christianity in both Egypt and Mesopotamia, where churches flourished for centuries. Others read these verses as a vision of the final age, when the nations will worship God together, and hold that no historical period has fulfilled them fully. Some scholars read them as a later expansion reflecting the hopes of Jews in Egypt. The verse about the City of the Sun has its own textual question: most Hebrew manuscripts read City of Destruction, while the Dead Sea Isaiah Scroll and other witnesses read City of the Sun, probably Heliopolis near Memphis, which is the reading the BSB follows. What is clear is the text's own horizon: in that day, a time of God's future action, the enemies of God's people become his people. That is a vision the church has always understood as still unfolding.

questions: Egypt's wise men could not see what God was doing. What sources of wisdom do people today trust that might leave them unable to read the times?
The chapter calls Egypt My people and Assyria My handiwork, the nations that oppressed Israel. What does this say about how God sees your enemies?
God strikes Egypt in order to heal it. Have you ever experienced a hardship that turned you back to God?
